(CNN) -- Pirates captured a Belgian ship and said they were taking it to the coast of Somalia after the vessel was reported missing early Saturday, NATO and pirate sources told CNN. The Dutch frigate De Zeven Provincien tracked seven pirates Saturday back to their mother ship. The Pompei, a Belgian-registered ship believed to have a mostly Belgian and Croatian crew, was one of two vessels that came under attack near the Indian Ocean island nation of Seychelles on Saturday, the sources said. The second ship escaped the attack after a brief exchange of gunfire with pirate vessels, the pirate source added. Meanwhile, Dutch naval forces captured seven pirates and freed 20 captive fishermen after tracking the pirates to their "mother ship" in the western Gulf of Aden on Saturday, a NATO maritime spokesman said. The Belgian government tried to communicate with the Pompei "without success" before the ship was confirmed to have been hijacked, according to an official.  See an interactive map of 2009 pirate attacks off the Horn of Africa » . "This morning we received two different channels, a silent alert, that there was a problem on the boat, which is a Belgian boat on its way to Seychelles," Belgium Government Crisis Center spokesman Peter Martens told reporters. "We tried to have a contact with the ship but without success until now." The archipelago where the attack occurred is roughly 800 miles off the Somali coastline. "Somali pirates are getting wilder and out of control," pirate spokesman Ali Sugulle said on April 11. "They go too far away from the Somali [coast] and go to the Kenyan coast even." The European Union, NATO and the United States have been patrolling the waters off Somalia since an upsurge in piracy in the region last year. No NATO vessels were in the region at the time of the attack, said Cmdr. Chris Davies from NATO's Maritime Component Command Headquarters in Northwood, England. Meanwhile, the Dutch rescue operation happened after pirates launched an unsuccessful attack on petroleum tanker MT Handytankers Magic, NATO Cmdr. Chris Davies told CNN. The Dutch frigate De Zeven Provincien was with the NATO fleet patrolling the region. After the Dutch disarmed the pirates, they released them, Shona Lowe, a spokeswoman from the maritime headquarters, told CNN. Because the crew was on a NATO mission, they lacked the jurisdiction to hold them, according to reports. The MT Handytankers Magic is part of a fleet belonging to Handytankers, a company that distributes petroleum products in Europe, the Mediterranean, and the United States, according to the company's Web site. Last week pirates attacked a U.S.-flagged ship, the Maersk Alabama, off the Somali coast.  The crew regained control of the ship but the captain was taken hostage and held for five days on a lifeboat.  The crisis ended when U.S. Navy sharpshooters shot and killed three of the pirates who were holding the captain. Journalist Mohammed Amiin contributed to this report.

## Dutch Navy Scores Success in Gulf of Aden

In a more encouraging development for anti-piracy efforts, the Dutch frigate De Zeven Provincien successfully intercepted and neutralized a pirate operation in the Gulf of Aden, one of the busiest and most dangerous shipping lanes in the world. Naval forces aboard the frigate tracked seven suspected pirates back to their "mother ship"—a larger vessel, often a hijacked fishing boat or dhow, that pirates use as a floating base to launch attacks on passing commercial vessels using smaller, faster skiffs.

The operation resulted in the capture of all seven pirates, who were apprehended by Dutch naval personnel following the pursuit. Perhaps more significantly, the raid also led to the liberation of 20 fishermen who had been held captive aboard the mother ship, apparently forced to crew the vessel for the pirates' operations. The fishermen's nationalities were not immediately specified, though foreign fishing crews are frequently seized by Somali pirates and used both as hostages and as unwilling labor to help operate the mother ships from which attacks are staged.

The De Zeven Provincien is part of the ongoing international naval presence in the region, which includes warships from the European Union's Operation Atalanta, NATO's counter-piracy mission, and individual nations conducting their own patrols, all aimed at safeguarding one of the world's most critical maritime trade routes.

Taken together, these incidents paint a complex picture of the ongoing battle against Somali piracy. While international naval forces continue to notch tactical successes—such as the Dutch frigate's operation, which resulted in the capture of pirates and the rescue of captive fishermen—the pirates themselves continue to adapt and expand their operations, pushing further out to sea and targeting vessels in previously unaffected waters like those surrounding the Seychelles.

Maritime security analysts have long warned that the use of "mother ships"—larger vessels that can support smaller attack skiffs far from shore—has been a key factor enabling pirates to strike at such great distances from Somalia. This tactic effectively extends their range by hundreds of miles, transforming what was once a coastal nuisance into a threat spanning a significant portion of the Indian Ocean.

The hijacking of the Pompei, coupled with the attempted attack that was repelled through armed resistance, suggests that despite the presence of multinational naval task forces in the region, pirates continue to find opportunities to strike, particularly against vessels that lack armed security details or naval escorts. Meanwhile, the success of operations like the one carried out by the De Zeven Provincien demonstrates that when naval forces are able to respond quickly and decisively, they can achieve significant results—both in terms of capturing pirates and rescuing those held hostage.

As shipping companies and international navies continue to grapple with this evolving threat, the incidents highlight the ongoing tension between the pirates' expanding operational capabilities and the international community's efforts to protect vital shipping lanes and the vessels that traverse them.

# Somali Pirates Hijack Belgian Vessel Near Seychelles; NATO Forces Thwart Second Attack in Gulf of Aden

**By CNN Staff**

Somali pirates seized a Belgian-flagged cargo vessel near the Seychelles early Tuesday, adding to a string of maritime hijackings that have plagued the region for years, even as NATO naval forces successfully intervened in a separate attack in the Gulf of Aden, rescuing the crew before pirates could gain control of the ship.

The Belgian vessel, identified by maritime officials as a bulk carrier, was traveling through waters roughly 500 nautical miles northeast of the Seychelles when it was approached by armed men in small skiffs, according to the European Union Naval Force (EU NAVFOR), which monitors shipping lanes in the region.

"We received a distress call indicating the vessel had been boarded," an EU NAVFOR spokesperson said. "By the time naval assets could respond, the pirates had already taken control of the ship and its crew."

The vessel's crew, believed to number around a dozen sailors of mixed nationality, is now being held hostage, according to maritime security officials. The ship's cargo and final destination were not immediately disclosed. Belgian Foreign Ministry officials confirmed they were "closely monitoring the situation" and coordinating with international partners to secure the crew's safe release.

This marks the latest in a series of hijackings attributed to Somali pirate networks operating out of coastal towns in the semi-autonomous Puntland region, where weak governance and grinding poverty have long fueled piracy as a lucrative, if illegal, enterprise.

## NATO Intervenes in Second Attack

In a more encouraging development, NATO forces patrolling the Gulf of Aden intercepted a separate hijacking attempt hours later, rescuing the crew of a merchant vessel before pirates could establish control.

According to NATO's Maritime Command, a warship in the area responded swiftly after receiving an emergency alert from the targeted vessel. A helicopter was dispatched, followed by a boarding team, which engaged the pirates before they could secure the bridge.

"Our forces arrived in time to prevent what could have been another prolonged hostage situation," a NATO official said in a statement. "The crew is safe, and several suspects have been detained."

The suspected pirates were taken into custody and will be processed under international protocols governing piracy prosecutions, though officials noted that legal proceedings against captured pirates have historically been complicated by jurisdictional questions and the reluctance of some nations to prosecute.

## A Persistent Threat

The dual incidents underscore the persistent danger piracy poses to one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, through which a significant percentage of global trade — including oil shipments bound for Europe and Asia — passes annually.

Despite a multinational naval presence that includes NATO, EU NAVFOR, and independent deployments from countries such as the United States, China, and India, pirates have continued to adapt their tactics, striking further from the Somali coast and using hijacked fishing vessels as "mother ships" to extend their range deep into the Indian Ocean.

Maritime security analysts say ransom payments, sometimes reaching into the millions of dollars, continue to make piracy an attractive option for young men in a region with few economic alternatives.

"Until the underlying issues of governance and economic opportunity in Somalia are addressed, we will keep seeing these attacks," said one regional security analyst who tracks piracy trends. "Naval patrols can respond to attacks, but they can't eliminate the incentive structure that drives people to attempt them in the first place."

The International Maritime Bureau has urged commercial vessels transiting the region to adhere strictly to recommended safety corridors and to maintain heightened vigilance, particularly during early morning hours when most attacks have historically occurred.

Negotiations for the release of the Belgian ship's crew are expected to begin in the coming days, though officials cautioned that such processes can take weeks or even months to resolve. The shipping company that owns the vessel has not yet issued a public statement.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

**GULF OF ADEN** — Maritime security officials confirmed two separate piracy incidents occurred off the Horn of Africa within the same day, highlighting the persistent threat to commercial shipping in one of the world's busiest maritime corridors.

## Belgian-Flagged Vessel Seized

A Belgian-flagged cargo vessel was successfully hijacked by armed pirates approximately 80 nautical miles off the Somali coast in the early morning hours, according to the European Union Naval Force (EU NAVFOR) and industry sources monitoring the region.

The vessel, reportedly carrying a mixed cargo and a crew of over a dozen international sailors, was boarded by armed men operating from a skiff launched from a larger "mother ship" — a tactic commonly used by Somali pirate networks to extend their operational range into deeper waters.

Maritime security firms indicated the ship's crew activated distress signals before communications were cut off. The vessel's last known position placed it on a course toward the Somali coastline, a pattern consistent with previous hijackings where vessels are anchored near shore while ransom negotiations take place.

The shipping company has not yet released a statement, though maritime insurers and regional authorities are reportedly coordinating with Belgian diplomatic channels to establish contact with the pirates and confirm the crew's safety.

## Dutch Frigate Foils Second Attack

In a separate incident several hours later, a Dutch frigate operating under EU NAVFOR's Operation Atalanta intervened to repel an attempted hijacking targeting a merchant vessel transiting the same general shipping corridor.

According to naval sources, the warship received a distress call from the merchant vessel after it reported being approached by a suspected pirate skiff. The frigate, already patrolling nearby waters as part of coordinated escort operations, dispatched a helicopter and rigid-hull inflatable boats to intercept the threat.

Upon realizing naval forces were closing in, the suspected pirates reportedly abandoned the attack and fled, dumping suspected weapons and boarding ladders overboard — a common tactic used to avoid prosecution, as many regional legal frameworks require physical evidence of piracy equipment for detention.

No injuries were reported among the merchant vessel's crew, and the ship was able to continue its voyage under naval escort as a precaution.

## Renewed Concerns Over Regional Security

The dual incidents have reignited concerns among shipping industry stakeholders about the resurgence of piracy activity in the region, an area that saw a significant decline in successful attacks following intensified international naval patrols in the previous decade.

Analysts point to a combination of factors potentially driving the uptick, including instability in Somalia, reduced naval presence in certain periods, and opportunistic timing exploiting gaps in escorted convoy schedules.

EU NAVFOR has urged all vessels transiting the Gulf of Aden and the wider Somali basin to strictly adhere to Best Management Practices (BMP5) guidelines, including maintaining registration with regional reporting centers, ensuring citadels are operational, and maximizing transit speed through high-risk areas.

The International Maritime Bureau's Piracy Reporting Centre has confirmed it is tracking both incidents and will issue updated advisories to vessels currently transiting or scheduled to enter the region in coming days.

Further updates are expected as negotiations for the Belgian vessel's crew develop and as naval authorities release additional details on the thwarted attack.

*This is a developing story.*

# Somali Pirates Continue Hijacking Spree as International Navies Struggle to Contain Threat

**By CNN Staff**

Somali pirates have seized another vessel and its crew off the coast of East Africa, officials confirmed Tuesday, in the latest incident highlighting the persistent threat piracy poses to shipping lanes despite an increased international naval presence in the region.

## Cargo Ship Pompei Seized

The German-owned cargo ship Pompei was captured by armed pirates in the Gulf of Aden, according to maritime security officials. The vessel was reportedly boarded by a group of pirates operating from a "mother ship" — a larger vessel used to launch fast, smaller skiffs capable of chasing down commercial ships far from shore.

Details about the crew's nationality and condition remained unclear as negotiations were expected to begin between the ship's owners and the pirates, who typically demand ransoms ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars for the safe return of vessels and hostages.

"These groups have become increasingly sophisticated in their operations," said one maritime security analyst tracking the incident. "The use of mother ships allows them to strike far beyond Somalia's coastal waters, making interception extremely difficult."

## Dutch Navy Rescues Fishermen

In a separate but related development, the Dutch navy said it rescued a group of fishermen who had been held by suspected pirates. According to Dutch military officials, a navy vessel operating in the region intervened after receiving distress signals, freeing the fishermen and detaining several suspected pirates in the process.

A Dutch defense ministry spokesperson said the operation was part of ongoing efforts by the European Union's counter-piracy mission, which has patrolled the waters off Somalia in coordination with other international forces, including NATO and independent naval deployments from the United States, China, and India.

"Our forces remain committed to protecting freedom of navigation and preventing acts of piracy that threaten innocent seafarers," the spokesperson said, adding that the detained suspects would be processed according to international protocols governing piracy prosecutions.

## Pirates Defend Their Actions

Despite widespread condemnation, individuals claiming to speak for pirate networks have continued to defend their activities, framing them as a response to what they describe as the plunder of Somali waters by foreign fishing fleets and the dumping of toxic waste off the country's coastline — claims that have circulated for years amid Somalia's prolonged political instability.

"We do not consider ourselves sea bandits," one man identifying himself as a pirate spokesman told reporters by satellite phone. "We are simply patrolling our waters. Foreign vessels have stolen our fish and destroyed our livelihoods for years while the world did nothing. This is the only way we can survive."

Analysts caution that while grievances over illegal fishing and environmental damage may have played a role in the origins of Somali piracy in the early 2000s, the practice has since evolved into a highly organized criminal enterprise generating tens of millions of dollars annually, often financed by networks extending beyond Somalia's borders.

## International Response Continues

The incidents underscore the ongoing challenge facing the international community as it seeks to secure one of the world's busiest shipping corridors. An estimated 20,000 vessels pass through the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean region each year, carrying goods between Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.

Naval coalitions, including the EU's Operation Atalanta, NATO's counter-piracy task force, and independent deployments, have had some success in deterring attacks through convoy escorts and patrols. However, officials acknowledge that the vast area of ocean involved makes complete protection impossible.

"We cannot police every mile of these waters," a Western naval official said. "As long as piracy remains profitable and Somalia continues to face internal instability, we will likely continue to see these kinds of incidents."

Shipping companies have increasingly turned to private armed security contractors and evasive maneuvering tactics to protect their vessels, while ransom insurance has become a standard part of doing business for many firms operating in high-risk waters.

The fate of the Pompei and its crew remained uncertain as of Tuesday evening, with negotiations expected to unfold over the coming weeks, a process that has, in past cases, taken months to resolve.

*CNN's coverage of maritime security and piracy in the Gulf of Aden continues to be updated as new information becomes available.*

# Piracy Surge Tests NATO Resolve in Horn of Africa Waters

**GULF OF ADEN** — The waters off Somalia's coast continued to churn with maritime peril this month, as a fresh wave of pirate attacks strained international naval forces and underscored the persistent vulnerability of commercial shipping lanes critical to global trade.

## A Belgian Vessel Vanishes

Among the most alarming incidents was the disappearance of a Belgian-flagged dredging vessel, the *Pompei*, which lost contact with maritime authorities while transiting waters near the Seychelles. The ship, operated by a Belgian dredging company, had been en route on a commercial contract when it stopped responding to radio communications, triggering immediate concern among European naval commands.

Maritime security officials feared the worst: another successful hijacking by Somali pirate gangs who have increasingly ventured farther from the Somali coastline, exploiting a vast expanse of ocean that no naval force—however well-resourced—could fully patrol. The incident renewed criticism that the pirates' operational range had outpaced the international response, with skiffs and mother ships now striking targets hundreds of miles from shore.

## NATO's Stretched Thin Presence

NATO's counter-piracy mission, part of a broader multinational effort that includes European Union naval forces, American warships, and vessels from India, China, and Russia, found itself confronting an uncomfortable arithmetic: the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean piracy zone span roughly 1.1 million square miles, an area alliance officials have likened to policing a landmass the size of Western Europe with a handful of patrol cars.

Despite establishing a designated Internationally Recommended Transit Corridor through the Gulf of Aden—meant to concentrate naval escorts and reduce risk for merchant traffic—pirates continued to demonstrate an ability to strike both within and beyond this protected channel. NATO commanders acknowledged that warships could respond to distress calls but often arrived too late, given the vast distances and the speed with which pirate skiffs could board and seize a vessel.

## A Tanker Fights Back

Not every attack succeeded, however. In one notable incident, a tanker came under assault from pirates wielding rocket-propelled grenades and automatic weapons, only to escape capture through a combination of evasive maneuvering, onboard security measures, and the intervention of a nearby warship responding to the crew's distress signal.

The tanker's crew, following increasingly standardized guidance from maritime security advisories, had taken defensive precautions—reportedly including the use of fire hoses to repel boarders and retreating to a fortified "citadel" area of the ship, a tactic that had grown more common among merchant crews transiting the danger zone. The pirates, unable to board before naval or private security assets arrived, ultimately abandoned the pursuit.

## A Pattern Repeating

Maritime analysts noted that April's events fit a grim seasonal pattern: pirate activity typically intensified as weather conditions in the Indian Ocean improved, allowing skiffs launched from larger "mother ships" to operate farther offshore with greater endurance. The International Maritime Bureau's piracy reporting center in Kuala Lumpur had already logged dozens of attacks and hijackings for the year, with ransom payments—some reportedly reaching into the millions of dollars—continuing to fund more sophisticated pirate operations based in Somali coastal towns like Eyl and Haradheere.

For shipping companies, insurers, and the naval coalition alike, the month's events reinforced a sobering consensus: absent a political and economic solution addressing the collapse of governance in Somalia itself, naval patrols—however international, however well-coordinated—could manage the crisis but not resolve it. The disappearance of the *Pompei*, whatever its ultimate fate, stood as a stark reminder that in these waters, even vigilance offered no guarantee of safety.
